extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in health communication, social media scholars, public health communicators, and computational social scientists
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, coding, clustering, and evaluating multi-element health messages on social media using the SAFE (Source–Appeal–Frame–Evidence) framework and large-scale engagement metrics (likes/comments/shares). Includes methodological standards for data selection, coding, clustering, and statistical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAFE framework (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat health messages as combinations across four theoretical dimensions: Source, Appeal, Frame, and Evidence (Source–Appeal–Frame–Evidence). Code each post on these four dimensions to capture multi-element composition rather than isolated cues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SAFE categories and conceptual definitions as an explicit codebook; each post is coded across all four dimensions and a post may contain multiple features in a dimension (multi-label). The framework underpins representation, clustering, and interpretation of recurring message patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source dimension (SAFE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify source cues into categories: Expert (Exp), Official Media (OffM), or No Source (NoSrc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert: results/analyses from recognized professionals, scholars, or authoritative institutions. Official Media: information published by government, public health agencies, or credible news media. No Source: lack of clear or identifiable source support. Use these categories to anchor credibility-centered baselines (e.g., Institutional Authority Pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal dimension (SAFE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify appeals into types: Sex (Sex), Fear (Fear), Humor (Humor), Value (Valu), Utilitarian (Util), Dual (Dual), Comparative (Comp), Metaphor (Met), or No Appeal (NoApp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Sex = attraction/sensual cues; Fear = emphasizing negative consequences; Humor = ironic/positive emotional; Value = prosocial/normative appeals; Utilitarian = functional benefits/efficacy; Dual = presenting both supporting and opposing viewpoints; Comparative = comparing alternatives; Metaphor = figurative expressions; NoApp = no clear appeal. Use appeal types to evaluate affective vs informational prompting and to identify alignment with baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame dimension (SAFE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize framing as Gain (highlight benefits), Loss (emphasize risks), or No Frame (NoFrm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame interacts with appeals and evidence (e.g., fear appeals in loss frames, hope appeals in gain frames). Capture framing because it guides interpretation and conditions how appeals/evidence operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence dimension (SAFE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify evidence as Narrative (NarrEv), Statistical (StatEv), Expert (ExpEv), Causal (CausEv), or No Evidence (NoEv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative = stories/experiences; Statistical = numerical/aggregated data; Expert = references to expert opinion/research; Causal = descriptions of cause–effect. Evidence type conditions credibility and sharing (e.g., statistical evidence benefits from credible sources; narrative evidence compensates for weak source cues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data inclusion and selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Select posts from verified/certified health science bloggers; retrieve first-level original posts (exclude reposts/forwards); include standard posts and extended long-form posts (Changweibo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify certified health science bloggers using platform verification and domain classifications (example: Weibo's top-ranked health bloggers list). Use API scripts to retrieve full text; retain only original content to reflect message construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprocessing and health-content filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply multi-step preprocessing: remove duplicates and non-original posts; use a BERT-based classifier to retain health-related content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure data quality before coding. Preprocessing choices affect representativeness; document classifier details and any thresholds used.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-assisted coding and codebook usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use GPT-assisted (e.g., GPT-5) deductive coding with SAFE categories and embedded conceptual definitions in prompts; treat these definitions as the explicit codebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine AI-assisted coding with human oversight: provide definitions in prompts, run reliability checks, and report human–AI agreement statistics. Keep the codebook available for replication and auditing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercoder reliability standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess reliability using human coders on a stratified random sample; report intercoder agreement statistics (Cohen’s κ, accuracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example standard in the paper: 1,000 posts coded by two trained graduate coders; Cohen’s κ = 0.78 and human–GPT accuracy ≈ 83.5% considered acceptable. Report sample size for reliability test and how human–AI agreement was measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of posts for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent each post as a multi-label feature vector indicating presence/absence of SAFE elements; allow multiple features per dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the multi-label vectors (not raw text embeddings) when clustering to identify recurring element combinations and co-occurrence patterns rather than topics or semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clustering approach for message combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cluster on coded SAFE feature vectors using HDBSCAN to detect dense regions without pre-specifying the number of clusters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HDBSCAN identifies dense clusters and classifies noise; fit model on repeated subsamples for efficiency and extend to the full dataset via approximate prediction. Document HDBSCAN parameters and subsampling strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster validation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate clusters using cosine similarity (within-pattern similarity should exceed between-pattern similarity) and report statistics (e.g., global average, within-pattern ranges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example thresholds/results: global avg similarity = 0.43 (SD=0.18); within-pattern similarity ranged 0.60–0.66. Report subgroup similarities (e.g., cluster pair similarities) to support aggregation into higher-order patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication-effect metrics and transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use likes, comments, and shares as observable indicators of communication effects; due to skew, log-transform metrics using log(x + 1) for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that likes/comments/shares are indirect proxies for attention, endorsement, interaction, and diffusion and do not directly measure attitude or behavior change. Use transformed metrics for stable comparisons and report transformation explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source visibility operationalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalize source influence (visibility) by grouping follower counts into distribution-based tiers: top 10%, middle (50th–90th percentile), and bottom 50%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tiering to compare visibility conditions; validate classification (e.g., report mean follower counts per tier and ANOVA results showing significant separation). Justify why tiering was chosen over treating follower count as continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and estimation of ΔE (effect difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ΔE as the difference in mean log-transformed communication-effect indicators between posts with baseline+S (additional peripheral elements) and posts with the baseline only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ΔE to quantify association of added element combinations with effects. Report ΔE for likes, comments, and shares separately and interpret direction and magnitude accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical reporting thresholds for combination effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Report only element combinations with sample size N > 300 and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals that do not cross zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bootstrap resampling (example: n = 500) to compute 95% CIs; the N>300 threshold reduces influence of small cell sizes and the CI criterion ensures reported associations are statistically stable (less likely to be noise). Display representative combinations (e.g., via Venn-style visualizations) only under these criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bootstrap uncertainty estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bootstrap resampling (example: n = 500) to estimate statistical uncertainty and compute 95% confidence intervals for ΔE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bootstrapping is recommended for skewed engagement distributions. Report the number of bootstrap iterations and how CIs were computed; use bootstrap standard errors in plots and CI-based decision rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core–Periphery–Environment (C–P–E) framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Model message patterns as core baselines (typically two core elements) with peripheral elements that modify effectiveness and environmental conditions (e.g., source influence) that condition which combinations are effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat core structures as stable persuasive logics (e.g., Institutional Authority: source+evidence); peripheral elements can reinforce (synergy) or conflict (trade-off) with cores. Use framework to guide both analysis and practical message design, understanding that it is an explanatory/middle-range framework rather than a causal model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripheral complexity guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderate peripheral complexity—typically adding two to four peripheral elements beyond the baseline—tends to be associated with stronger communication effects; beyond four shows diminishing returns or stabilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate ΔE by number of added elements (k) and compare across patterns and indicators. Use this guideline when designing messages: moderate complexity often outperforms minimal or excessive complexity, but optimal k may vary by baseline and source influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synergy versus trade-off principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripheral elements can produce synergistic effects when aligned with baseline logic (reinforcement) or trade-offs when they conflict with it (incompatibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the study: In Institutional Authority Pattern (IAP), metaphor + utilitarian + narrative + value positively associated with likes/shares; NoApp + NoFrm is negative. In Narrative Pattern (NP), humor and contrastive appeals are positive, while adding expert evidence (ExpEv) can reduce effectiveness (trade-off). In Assertive Appeal Pattern (AAP), strengthening appeals (dual, humor) increases likes/comments; value+utilitarian helps shares. In Contextual Expression Pattern (CEP), stronger elements often show limited gains and official media cues may be negatively associated. Use alignment tests (ΔE with bootstrap CIs) to detect synergy/trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern-specific practical messaging recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Match communication goals to baseline patterns and align peripheral elements with baseline logic: IAP (credibility-centered) benefits from credibility + interpretable/relatable elements; NP (narrative-centered) benefits from emotional coherence and may be weakened by analytical/expert cues; AAP (appeal-driven without explicit source/evidence) benefits immediate reactions from affective appeals but needs utility/value for sharing; CEP (low-intensity) is better served by simple combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice: authority-based messages should combine credibility with value or utilitarian elements; narrative messages should avoid conflicting analytical evidence and instead add metaphor/humor/value; low-intensity informational posts should prioritize clarity and minimal structure. Also adapt strategies to source influence: high-visibility accounts can use simpler combos; low-visibility accounts may need more elaborate combinations to compensate.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-assisted content generation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When using AI for content generation, incorporate structured element combinations: select a baseline pattern, align peripheral elements with its logic, and adjust peripheral complexity according to source influence and communication goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template- and prompt-based AI systems can operationalize the C–P–E framework: specify the baseline (e.g., IAP), enumerate permissible peripheral elements (2–4 preferred), and set constraints to avoid combinations known to conflict (e.g., NP + ExpEv). Document prompt schemas and guardrails to prevent misaligned combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and transparency standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Document and report data selection, preprocessing, coding procedures (including AI-assistance prompts/codebook), reliability statistics, clustering parameters, validation metrics, and the exact thresholds used for reporting combinations and effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency enables replication and proper interpretation: report number of posts, noise proportion from clustering, cluster sizes, subsampling strategy, bootstrapping details (iterations), and all inclusion/exclusion thresholds (e.g., N>300).
